title: The hierarchy of controls for height work
audience: Workers, leading hands and supervisors who choose how a height task will be controlled.
learningOutcomes: Order the height-work controls by how dependable they are.
Explain why personal arrest equipment is a later choice than a physical control or avoidance.
Apply the hierarchy to a worked service job and record the reason for each level chosen or rejected.
Recognise when a lower-level control is being used because a higher level was not checked.

instruction.heading: Why the controls are ranked
instruction.body: Controls differ in how much they depend on people doing the right thing every time. A control that removes the fall exposure works whether a worker is tired, rushed or inexperienced. A control that only tells people what to do depends on their attention at each moment. The Victorian regulator sets out a ranking that begins with eliminating the hazard and ends with personal protective equipment. The training and contractor sources in this pack use the same idea with different words: first stop the need to go to height, then stop the fall, then limit what a fall can do, and only then rely on personal equipment and procedure.

instruction.heading: The levels, from the top
instruction.body: The top level is avoidance: do the work from the ground, use an extension tool, build components at ground level and lift them into place, or change the design so no access is needed. The next level is physical prevention: guardrails, edge protection, covers over openings, a fully boarded platform with rails, or a scaffold. Below that sits restraint, which stops a worker reaching the edge at all. Arrest comes next. It accepts that a fall can start and stops it through a harness and an energy-absorbing device. Every level depends on a rescue plan that is ready before the work starts. One source calls fall arrest the final layer of protection, and another ranks restraint as the safest personal option. The Victorian page places personal protective equipment lowest, as the least dependable control, to be used only when nothing else fits, as an interim measure, or alongside a higher control.

instruction.heading: Mapping the order to the Australian framework
instruction.body: The order above is a working ranking for this course. Where a business writes the control into a formal risk register, it should map each control to the level of the hierarchy used in the state or territory where the work happens. The practical rule holds regardless: a personal harness is the lowest of the physical choices and is never a substitute for a guardrail or a ground-based method that can be used.

instruction.heading: Applying the order to a job
instruction.body: Start at the top of the list for every job, and move down only with a written reason. A written reason can be checked later, and an unwritten one cannot. In practice, gutter cleaning should move to ground-based equipment where a suitable tool exists. If it does not, a guardrail or a stable platform goes in place. If neither is feasible, a restraint keeps the worker clear of the edge. Only when all of those are excluded should an arrest system be used, with its clearance checked and a rescue plan ready. A harness should not be the first control just because it is easy to carry.

instruction.heading: Engineered controls are not automatic
instruction.body: A guardrail counts as a control only if it is complete, fixed and at the right height. A platform counts only if its decking is full and secure. A higher control can be written into a plan and not be on site, so check each control on arrival and record what was seen. A plan that names a guardrail that is not fitted is not a plan with a guardrail.

instruction.heading: Administrative controls support the physical ones
instruction.body: Training, permits, supervision, signs and barriers manage people. They do not change the fall itself. Training and supervision matter, and the sources insist on both, but they cannot replace a physical control where falling is possible. A warning sign at the foot of a ladder is a reminder, not an edge guard, and it must not be the only control for a fall exposure.

procedure: List every fall exposure in the task.
Ask whether the task can be done from the ground or with no access at all, and record the answer.
If not, ask whether a guardrail, a complete platform or a cover can stop the fall, and check it on site.
If not, ask whether a restraint can keep the worker clear of the edge, and check its anchor.
If not, select arrest equipment, confirm the clearance below, and confirm the rescue plan.
Record the chosen control and every higher level rejected, with the reason for each.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner must wash a high window on a two-storey building. A telescopic pole system can reach the glass from the ground.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which level should be tried first, and what must be written down?
workedExamples.reasoning: Avoidance is the top level. Only if a ground-based method cannot reach the required standard should the job move down. The reason for moving down is written, and the ground-based method is recorded as the first option considered.

workedExamples.situation: A roofer must fix a ridge capping on a pitched roof. There is no guardrail, and the eave is about four metres above a path.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What change to the plan is needed before any harness is used?
workedExamples.reasoning: A physical edge control, such as a guardrail, a parapet or a platform, must be considered before a harness. A harness alone is a low-level choice, and the rescue plan has to be ready before the roof is accessed. The plan should record why each physical option was rejected.

equipmentAndPpe: A written job plan showing the control chosen at each level
Guardrail, edge protection or scaffold where a physical control is chosen (see “Edge protection, floor openings and covers”)
Restraint or arrest equipment only after the higher levels are excluded (see “Fall protection and arrest systems”)

commonErrors.error: Going straight to a harness because it is in the van.
commonErrors.prevention: Work down the order and write the reason for each step that is rejected.

commonErrors.error: Listing a guardrail in the plan that is not actually fitted.
commonErrors.prevention: Inspect each physical control on arrival and record what was seen.

commonErrors.error: Treating a warning sign as the control for a fall exposure.
commonErrors.prevention: Use signs and barriers to support a physical control, never in place of one.

commonErrors.error: Choosing a higher-level control that does not fit the work.
commonErrors.prevention: Check fit, access and the route before the control is chosen.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Warning: personal fall protection is the lowest level of most hierarchies. Do not use it as the only control where a physical control can be fitted.
The Victorian ranking is taken from a regulator page checked on 2026-11-02.
Stop-work rule: if the higher control cannot be fitted or checked, stop, report the problem and record it.

Licence notice: choosing a control does not grant a licence or any authority to work at height or to use access equipment. Where a state rule requires a licence for a platform or scaffold, the licence governs and is covered in “Scaffold and mobile tower checks before use” and “Elevated work platform pre-use checks”.

qualityStandard: The control chosen is the highest level that can be checked on site.
Every rejected higher level has a written reason.
Each physical control named is checked on arrival.
documentationEvidence: Control selection record showing rejected levels and reasons
Arrival check record for each physical control
summary: Start at the top of the order and move down only with a written reason.
Physical controls and avoidance outrank personal equipment.
A control in a plan is not a control until it is on site and checked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of these sits highest in the order described in this lesson?
options: A personal fall-arrest harness with a lanyard and a spare harness in the van
Avoiding the need to work at height, for instance by working from the ground
A written permit and a supervisor's instructions and a copy kept in the van
A warning sign placed at the foot of a ladder and a cone on the path

knowledgeChecks.question: A guardrail can be fitted to a roof edge. Why is it generally a stronger choice than a harness alone?
options: It is lighter to carry up a ladder and it is cheaper than most harnesses and easy to fit
It stops a person reaching the edge or falling, so it does not depend on each worker making the correct move.
It needs no inspection and the crew can skip the checks at the start of every single day on the job
It replaces the need for any rescue plan and the crew does not need any training or the harness

knowledgeChecks.question: A supervisor wants to skip a higher control on a job. What must happen first?
options: Ask the client to sign a waiver and the waiver is kept in the van for the whole job and the week after
Write the reason the higher control is not feasible, and choose a control one level up that can be checked on site.
Skip the record because the job is short and the crew knows what to do already and the team agrees
Use the lowest control and tell the team afterwards and the crew will check it later that day
